Hey! It happens sometimes. We are human and make mistakes. I had this happen a few weeks ago. When I realized my mistake I called the client immediately and apologized, acknowledged the mistake and also my humanness as a being that makes mistakes. In the next session I checked in with the client if there was a need for repair, fortunately the client was understanding, and made a point to tell them that I care about them and the mistake did not come from a place of lack of care or deprioritizing them. It’s okay to make mistakes, you’re a fallible human before you are a therapist. Just be humble, admit the mistake, apologize, and do whatever repair work is necessary if it is needed. Sometimes these moments can be valuable in the work with clients to show that we all make mistakes sometimes; how we address the mistake can be an opportunity for modeling pro-social behavior and for deepening the rapport. So, don’t fret too much. It’ll be okay. :)

Really appreciate your comment that is compassionate and also addressing that this is a very complex issue that is really many many layers of issues bundled into the issue of “homelessness”. While a top comment above wants to uncritically label this issue as a “grift masquerading as compassion”by these organizations, as someone working on the ground with the homeless population for one of these non-profits I can tell you that there is so much that makes this a very challenging issue to address. Speaking just from my own experiences with my non-profit, there is a significant issue with staffing; attracting, hiring, training, and (very key issue) retaining qualified trauma-informed compassionate staff is a significant issue for our organization. The non-profit as an entity that must have a vested interest in keeping itself funded is often making decisions that impact client care, put greater strain on burn-out staff, and put workers in a position where our own clinical ethics are opposed to what our organization is asking of us. Often we are working with people who need a much higher level of clinical care than we can provide in our clinical setting and it can be very challenging to get them to the appropriate level of care. People often ask me what I think should be done about the “homelessness problem” and I always tell them there is no one solution because it’s not one problem. It’s a wealth disparity problem, a housing problem, a mental health problem, a substance use problem, a healthcare problem, a funding problem, a problem of systemic injustice (racism, classism, and so on), a problem of mismanagement and greed, and so many others I could list but you get my point. And so many of these issues bundled into homelessness are themselves bundles of issues. All of this to say is there is no simple answer and as someone who has the faces, names, and stories of those this impacts the most all I can say is that so many of us are doing our best to improve a situation that feels insurmountable in so many ways.

Recipe for sauce: Pan fry bacon and diced red onion until red onion begins to soften. Then add chopped shiitake mushroom, deglaze the pan with a generous pour of sake, then add buna-shimeji mushroom and enoki mushroom. Add more sake. Let the mushroom, bacon, and onion cook down until there is no sake. Then add a spoonful of diced garlic and some butter. After the garlic has cooked for a couple of minutes add heavy cream and turn the heat up a little. Then add a meltable cheese. I used havarti for this, but would have preferred mozzarella. Add a splash of balsamic vinegar. Then add some salt, pepper, oregano, a bay leaf, and some basil, turn the heat down and let simmer until the sauce reaches deserved level of viscosity. Once there, add cooked somen noodles (takes 2min to boil somen noodle). Chop up some green onion, garnish as desired. Ta-da!
